title: Severe bleeding
recognize: Blood that is spurting, pouring, or pooling
Blood soaking through clothing or bandages
A deep or gaping wound
do_first: Press hard directly on the wound with a clean cloth, clothing, or a bare hand. Keep pressing without lifting to look.
If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top and press harder. Do not remove the first layer.

If life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg does not stop with direct pressure, apply a tourniquet 2 to 3 inches (5 to 8 cm) above the wound, not over a joint. Tighten until the bleeding stops and note the time.
Once bleeding is controlled, bandage firmly, keep the person lying down and keep them warm.
do_not: Do not remove an object that is stuck in the wound; pad around it
Do not keep lifting the dressing to check
Do not loosen or remove a tourniquet once it is on
escalate_when: Bleeding does not stop after 10 minutes of firm pressure
A tourniquet was needed
The person is pale, cold, sweaty, confused, or faint
The wound is to the chest, belly, neck, or groin

title: Hypothermia (dangerously cold)
recognize: Shivering that will not stop
Stumbling, fumbling hands, slurred or mumbled speech
Confusion, unusual behaviour, or wanting to lie down and sleep
Severe: shivering has stopped, very drowsy, or unresponsive
do_first: Get out of wind, rain, and snow. Use any shelter: tent, tarp, trees, a vehicle.
Gently replace wet clothing with dry layers. Cover the head and neck.
Insulate from the ground with a pad, pack, or branches, then wrap in a sleeping bag, blankets, or a tarp.
If fully alert and able to swallow, give warm sweet drinks and high-energy food.
Put warm (not hot) water bottles or heat packs, wrapped in cloth, on the chest, armpits, and groin.
Handle gently and keep the person lying flat if they are drowsy or confused.
do_not: Do not give alcohol
Do not rub or massage the arms and legs
Do not give food or drink to someone who is drowsy or confused
Do not put the person in a hot bath or right next to a fire
Do not let a confused or stumbling person keep walking
escalate_when: Confusion, slurred speech, or stumbling
Shivering has stopped but the person is still cold
Drowsy, hard to wake, or unresponsive
No improvement after an hour of rewarming

title: Heat exhaustion and heat stroke
recognize: Heat exhaustion: heavy sweating, headache, dizziness, nausea, cramps, weakness
Heat stroke (emergency): confusion, odd behaviour, collapse, seizure, or very hot skin
do_first: Stop all activity and move into shade.
Loosen or remove extra clothing.
Cool the person: wet the skin and clothing and fan them. Put cool wet cloths on the neck, armpits, and groin.
If fully alert, have them sip water, with electrolytes or a salty snack if available.
If they are confused, collapsed, or seizing, treat it as heat stroke: cool them as fast as you can, with cool-water immersion if there is safe water nearby, and keep cooling.
do_not: Do not let the person keep hiking
Do not give fluids to someone who is confused, drowsy, or vomiting
Do not leave the person alone
escalate_when: Confusion, slurred speech, or unusual behaviour
Collapse, fainting, or seizure
Vomiting that keeps them from drinking
No improvement after 30 minutes of rest and cooling

title: Head injury
recognize: A blow to the head followed by headache, dizziness, nausea, or feeling dazed
Memory gaps or repeating the same questions
Any loss of consciousness, even brief
do_first: Stop activity and have the person rest.
If the hit was hard or they fell from a height, assume the neck may be injured: keep the head and neck still.
Control any scalp bleeding with gentle, firm pressure.
Stay with them and check them often: are they alert, making sense, moving normally? Wake them every few hours overnight.
If they become unresponsive but are breathing, roll them onto their side while supporting the head and neck.
do_not: Do not leave the person alone
Do not let them continue climbing, riding, or hiking difficult terrain that day
Do not give alcohol or sedating medication
Do not press on a skull that feels soft or dented
escalate_when: Loss of consciousness, or growing drowsiness
Headache that keeps getting worse
Repeated vomiting
Confusion, slurred speech, or unusual behaviour
Seizure, weakness, numbness, or unequal pupils
Clear fluid or blood from the nose or ears

title: Sprain, fracture, or injured limb
recognize: Pain, swelling, or bruising after a fall or twist
Cannot use the limb or put weight on it
Limb looks bent or out of shape, or you heard a snap
do_first: Stop and take weight off the limb.
Check beyond the injury: can they feel your touch, wiggle fingers or toes, and is the skin warm and pink?
Splint it in a comfortable position with padding and something rigid (trekking poles, sticks, a sleeping pad), holding the joints above and below the injury still.
Cover any open wound with a clean dressing before splinting.
Raise the limb and cool it with cold water or snow wrapped in cloth, 20 minutes at a time.
Recheck feeling, movement, and colour after splinting and every so often after.
do_not: Do not force a bent limb straight
Do not push a bone end back into a wound
Do not tie the splint so tight that fingers or toes go numb, cold, or blue
Do not let them walk on a leg that cannot take weight
escalate_when: Bone showing through the skin
Fingers or toes beyond the injury are numb, cold, pale, or blue
The limb is clearly out of shape
The injury is to the thigh, hip, pelvis, back, or neck
They cannot bear any weight and you are far from the trailhead

title: Severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis)
recognize: After a sting, food, or medication: swelling of the lips, tongue, face, or throat
Trouble breathing, wheezing, or a tight throat
Hives over large areas, vomiting, dizziness, or collapse
do_first: If they have an epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen), use it now in the outer mid-thigh. It can go through clothing.
Lay them down with legs raised. If breathing is hard, let them sit up instead.
If there is no improvement after 5 to 15 minutes and a second auto-injector is available, give the second dose.
If it was a sting, scrape the stinger off.
Stay with them and watch their breathing. Symptoms can come back hours later.
do_not: Do not wait to see if it gets better before using epinephrine
Do not rely on antihistamine tablets alone for a severe reaction
Do not let them stand up or walk
escalate_when: Any trouble breathing or swelling of the throat or tongue
Epinephrine was used, even if they now feel better
Dizziness, fainting, or collapse
No epinephrine is available

title: Unresponsive person and CPR
recognize: Does not respond when you shout and tap their shoulders
Not breathing, or only gasping now and then
do_first: Make sure it is safe to approach, then shout and tap their shoulders.
Send someone for help and for an AED if one could be nearby.
Tilt the head back and check breathing for no more than 10 seconds.
Not breathing normally: start CPR. Push hard and fast on the centre of the chest, about 2 inches (5 cm) deep, 100 to 120 pushes a minute.
After every 30 pushes give 2 rescue breaths if you are able to. If not, keep pushing without stopping.
Use an AED as soon as one arrives and follow its voice prompts.
Breathing normally but unresponsive: roll them onto their side and keep watching their breathing.
do_not: Do not stop CPR to recheck for longer than 10 seconds
Do not give food or drink
Do not leave an unresponsive person lying on their back unattended
escalate_when: Always: an unresponsive person needs emergency help by any means available

title: Burns
recognize: Red, painful skin, or blisters after contact with heat
Deep burns may look white, leathery, or charred and hurt less
do_first: Stop the burning: move away from the heat, and smother flames on clothing.
Cool the burn with cool running water for 20 minutes. Clean stream or bottle water is fine.
Remove rings, watches, and tight clothing near the burn before it swells.
Cover loosely with a clean non-stick dressing or clean plastic wrap.
Keep the rest of the person warm while you cool the burn.
do_not: Do not use ice or ice water
Do not put butter, oil, toothpaste, or ointment on a fresh burn
Do not pop blisters
Do not pull off clothing that is stuck to the burn
escalate_when: The burn is larger than the person's palm and blistered or deep
Burns to the face, hands, feet, genitals, or over a joint
Burns that go all the way around a limb
Burns from electricity, lightning, or chemicals
Breathing trouble, a hoarse voice, or soot around the mouth and nose

title: Snakebite
recognize: A bite from a snake, with or without visible fang marks
Pain, swelling, or bruising that spreads from the bite
Nausea, weakness, tingling, or trouble breathing
do_first: Move away from the snake. Do not try to catch or kill it.
Keep the person calm and as still as possible.
Remove rings, watches, and tight clothing from the bitten limb before it swells.
Keep the bitten limb still, in a comfortable position.
Mark the edge of the swelling on the skin and write the time next to it.
Start getting the person to medical care. Antivenom is the treatment, and it is only available at a hospital.
do_not: Do not cut the bite
Do not try to suck out the venom
Do not apply a tourniquet
Do not apply ice
Do not give alcohol
escalate_when: Always: any suspected venomous snakebite needs evacuation to a hospital
